1. Cardiac Electrical Properties

Ventricular Myocyte Action Potential

Ventricular myocyte action potential phases
  • Phase 4 (resting, −90 mV): high K⁺ permeability; Na⁺/Ca²⁺ channels closed
  • Phase 0 (upstroke): voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open, AP peaks at +30 mV
  • Phase 1 (initial repolarization): Na⁺ channels inactivate, K⁺ channels begin opening
  • Phase 2 (plateau): Ca²⁺ influx (L-type channels) balances K⁺ efflux — triggers Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release & contraction. CCBs act here — block L-type Ca²⁺ channels, shortening the plateau + contraction
  • Phase 3 (rapid repolarization): massive K⁺ efflux, Ca²⁺ channels close
CCB effects on the heart: ↓ SA node discharge rate, ↓ AV conduction, ↓ HR, ↓ contractility, overall ↓ conduction. Classes: dihydropyridines (nifedipine, amlodipine), benzothiazepine (diltiazem), phenylalkylamine (verapamil).

Channelopathies: Long QT — K⁺ channels slower/longer to open → longer plateau. AFib — K⁺ channels open faster → quicker repolarization/electrical cycle.

Refractory period is longer in cardiac than skeletal muscle (long plateau) — prevents tetany, allows fill/contract cycling. ARP = no further depolarization possible; RRP = stronger-than-normal stimulus can trigger one.

Excitation-Contraction Coupling

  • Calcium-induced calcium release: AP → L-type (DHP) receptors open → Ca²⁺ entry → triggers SR Ca²⁺ release via ryanodine receptors → Ca²⁺ binds troponin-C → actin-myosin cross-bridging
  • SERCA2A (cardiac isoform) actively pumps Ca²⁺ back into SR; phospholamban (PLB) inhibits SERCA when unphosphorylated. PKA phosphorylates PLB → dissociates → ↑SERCA activity → ↑Ca²⁺ reuptake

Conduction System

SA node pacemaker action potential (funny current)
  • Pathway: SA node → atrial myocardium → AV node → AV bundle (His) → Purkinje fibers → ventricular myocardium
  • Intrinsic rates: SA node 70–80/min > AV node 40–60/min > Purkinje 15–40/min
  • Conduction velocities: SA node 0.5 m/s → AV node 0.05 m/s (slowest — allows ventricular filling) → Bundle of His ~2 m/s → Purkinje fibers ~4 m/s (fastest)
  • SA node lacks a stable resting potential — starts at −60 mV, slow depolarization via the funny current (If) (slow Na⁺ leak) = phase 4; at −40 mV, L-type Ca²⁺ channels open (phase 0, peaks at 0 mV); K⁺ channels then repolarize to ~−55 mV (phase 3)
  • Ectopic beats: atrial → early/abnormal P wave + normal QRS; ventricular → wide QRS (>0.12s). Stokes-Adams syndrome = syncope ~20s after pacemaker pickup delay

Regulation of SA Node Rate

  • Autonomic activity: ↑sympathetic (β1, ↑cAMP → binds HCN channels → ↑If) = ↑HR
  • Serum K⁺: hyperkalemia → bradycardia (or arrest); hypokalemia → ↑phase 4 slope → tachycardia
  • Hypoxia → depolarizes membrane → bradycardia

2. The Normal ECG

ECG waveform: P wave, PR interval, QRS, ST segment, T wave
Wave/IntervalRepresentsNormal Value
P waveAtrial depolarization (precedes atrial contraction)—
PR intervalAV nodal delay allowing ventricular filling~160 ms (0.12–0.22s)
QRS complexVentricular depolarization (precedes ventricular contraction)<0.12s
ST segmentVentricular systole (plateau phase of myocyte AP)Isoelectric
T waveVentricular repolarization/relaxation—
QT intervalFull ventricular depolarization + repolarization~350 ms (≤0.45s)
HR = 60/R-R interval (sec). Normal R-R = 830ms → HR = 60/0.83 = 72 bpm.

Vectorial Analysis

  • Normal mean QRS axis = ~60° (range −30° to 110°) — lies almost along Lead II, so Lead II shows the most prominent +ve deflection
  • Current toward an electrode = positive (upward) deflection; current away = negative deflection (reverse for repolarization)
  • Ventricular depolarization starts at the septum/endocardium; net current flows base→apex

Limb Leads & Einthoven's Law

Bipolar limb leads and Einthoven's triangle
  • Einthoven's Law: Lead II = Lead I + Lead III (any 2 of the 3 bipolar limb leads determine the third)
  • Lead I: (+) left arm, (−) right arm. Lead II: (+) left leg, (−) right arm. Lead III: (+) left leg, (−) left arm
  • Augmented leads: aVL (−30°), aVR (−150°), aVF (+90°) — together with the 3 bipolar leads, form the 6 frontal-plane limb leads

Precordial Leads & Coronary Territories

Precordial (chest) leads V1–V6 — view the heart in a plane perpendicular to the frontal plane
ECG leads and corresponding coronary artery territories
e.g. ST elevation in Lead II = inferior wall MI — caused by RCA or LCX occlusion.

3. The Abnormal ECG

Systematic Interpretation Checklist

  • Rhythm: ~70 bpm normal via R-R interval; <60 = bradycardia, >100 = tachycardia
  • P wave/PR interval: positive in II, III, aVF normally; PR = 0.12–0.22s
  • QRS: <0.12s duration; amplitude >5mm (limb) / >10mm (chest) normal, >35mm = high voltage (hypertrophy); wide Q waves (>0.03s) suggest pathology
  • ST segment: isoelectric; deviation measured at the J point
  • QT interval: ≤0.45s; prolongation risks malignant arrhythmia

P-wave / PR Interval Disease — AV Blocks & WPW

  • 1° AV block: PR >0.2s, every P followed by QRS (delay, not a true block)
  • 2° AV block (Mobitz I/Wenckebach): progressively lengthening PR until a QRS is dropped
  • 2° AV block (Mobitz II): constant PR with intermittently dropped QRS (fixed ratios e.g. 2:1, 3:1)
  • 3° (complete) AV block: total dissociation — P waves and QRS complexes unrelated
  • WPW syndrome: accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent) bypasses the AV node → short PR + wide QRS + delta wave
  • RBBB: QRS >0.12s, V1 positive secondary R wave, V6 slurred terminal S wave (often right axis shift)
  • LBBB: QRS >0.12s, V1 wide negative S wave, V6 "rabbit ear" pattern (often left axis shift)

Voltage Changes

  • High voltage (sum of limb leads >4mV): usually ↑ventricular muscle mass (hypertrophy)
  • Low voltage: old infarcts (↓muscle mass) or pericardial fluid (conducts electricity, dampens signal)
  • HCM: ↑QRS amplitude ± narrowing

QRS Abnormalities

Narrow QRS (<100ms, supraventricular origin):

  • AFib: absent P waves + irregularly irregular rate ("circus movements")
  • Atrial flutter: reentrant circuit (cavotricuspid isthmus), atrial rate ~300/min, sawtooth F waves in II/III/aVF

Wide QRS (>100ms):

  • Causes: BBB, hyperkalemia, Na-channel blocker poisoning (TCAs), WPW, hypothermia
  • V-tach: ≥3 consecutive beats >100bpm from ventricle, always wide QRS
  • PVC: ectopic ventricular beat, wide QRS (>0.12s)
Premature ventricular contraction (PVC) — wide, bizarre QRS

Current of Injury

Transmural ischemia → ST elevation; subendocardial ischemia → ST depression
  • Damaged myocardium stays partially/fully depolarized → current flows even between beats; injured area is relatively negative
  • Transmural ischemia → ST elevation. Subendocardial ischemia → ST depression. Causes: local ischemia, trauma, infection

QT/T-Wave/U-Wave & Electrolytes

ECG changes in hypokalemia vs. hyperkalemia
  • Hypokalemia: flattened/inverted T waves → QT prolongation, visible U wave, mild ST depression (slowed repolarization)
  • Hyperkalemia: tall peaked T waves → widened QRS with reduced amplitude, flattened P wave (delayed repolarization/depolarization)
  • Hypercalcemia: shortens QT (facilitated Ca²⁺ entry abbreviates the plateau)

4. Cardiac Cycle & JVP

Wiggers Diagram

Wiggers diagram: pressure, volume, ECG, and heart sounds through one cardiac cycle
PhaseEvents
Ventricular diastoleVentricles expand, pressure < atria, AV valves open, EDV ~130 mL reached
Isovolumetric contractionMitral closes → aortic opens; ↑pressure, no volume change; S1 occurs (AV valve closure)
Ventricular ejectionAortic valve opens; LV pressure peaks ~120 mmHg (RV ~25 mmHg); volume ↓
Isovolumetric relaxationAortic closes → mitral opens; ↓pressure, no volume change; S2 occurs (semilunar closure)
Total cardiac cycle ~800ms at 75 bpm: atrial systole ~0.1s, ventricular systole ~0.3s, quiescent (all 4 chambers in diastole) ~0.4s.

Valve disease on Wiggers diagram: aortic regurgitation — dicrotic notch absent. Aortic stenosis — LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure during systole.

S3 = transition from rapid to slow ventricular filling (early diastole); S2 splitting = A2 normally closes before P2, abnormal splitting suggests disease.

Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP)

Normal JVP waveform: a, c, v waves and x, y descents
  • Normal mean JVP = 6–8 cm H₂O (above right atrium midpoint); <5 = hypovolemia, >9 = impaired cardiac filling
  • a wave = atrial contraction. c wave = tricuspid bulging into RA / carotid transmission. v wave = passive RA filling in late systole
  • x descent = atrial relaxation/downward pull during ventricular systole. y descent = tricuspid opens, rapid RV filling begins
Clinical correlations: Giant a waves = ↓RV compliance or tricuspid stenosis (causes: pulmonic stenosis, COPD with pulm. HTN, restrictive cardiomyopathy). Cannon a waves = atrial contraction against closed tricuspid valve (complete heart block). Slow y descent = tricuspid stenosis. Rapid x/y descents = constrictive pericarditis or RV failure.

5. Cardiac Output & PV Loops

CO = HR × SV. Normal resting CO = 5 L/min. Cardiac Index = CO/BSA (normal 2.6–4.2 L/min/m²).
  • SV = EDV − ESV (typical: 120mL − 50mL = 70mL)
  • 3 determinants of SV: Preload (EDV), Contractility, Afterload (resistance to ejection, mainly aortic/pulmonary pressure)
  • EF = SV/EDV × 100 — normal ~58–60%. HFrEF: EF ≤40% (reduced). HFpEF: normal EF but ventricle still in failure

PV Loop Mechanics

Basic LV pressure-volume loop
  • Mitral closes (EDV/preload) → isovolumetric contraction → aortic opens → ejection → aortic closes (ESV) → isovolumetric relaxation → mitral opens
  • ↑Preload → ↑EDV, ↑SV. ↑Afterload → ↑ESV, ↓SV. ↑Contractility → ↓ESV, ↑SV

Valve Disorders on PV Loops

PV loops: aortic/mitral regurgitation and stenosis
Valve LesionKey PV Loop Change
Mitral stenosis↓EDV (impaired filling) → ↓SV → ↓CO
Mitral regurgitation↓afterload (backflow to LA) → ↓ESV; ↑EDV from LA pressure → ↑total SV but ↓forward flow
Aortic stenosis↑outflow resistance → ↑afterload, ↑ESV, ↓SV
Aortic regurgitationDiastolic backflow into LV → ↑EDV (enhanced filling)

Systolic Heart Failure & Hypertrophy

Loss of inotropy → ↓ESPVR slope, ↑ESV, ↓SV, ↓EF
Hypertrophy → ↑EDPVR (↓compliance) → ↓SV over time
  • ESPVR = index of contractility — steeper slope = ↑contractility. Systolic HF ↓slope → ↑ESV, ↓SV, ↓EF
  • EDPVR = index of (1/compliance) — hypertrophy stiffens the ventricle (↑EDPVR), impairing diastolic filling → ↓SV over time

Chronotropic Regulation

  • Medullary cardiac centers: sympathetic (cardiostimulatory) vs. vagal/parasympathetic (cardioinhibitory)
  • Inputs: proprioceptors (anticipate exercise demand), baroreceptors (BP), chemoreceptors (pH/CO₂/O₂)
  • ACh → M2 receptors on SA node → ↓HR. Epinephrine → β1 receptors (higher affinity than NE) → ↑↑HR (fight-or-flight)

6. Venous Return & CO/VR Curves

  • CO is controlled by venous return — Frank-Starling law: ↑venous filling → ↑stretch → ↑force of contraction (ejects the extra volume)
  • Bainbridge reflex: atrial stretch receptors → ↑sympathetic outflow → ↑contractility
  • CO = (MAP − RAP)/TPR — at constant MAP, ↑TPR causes ↓CO (inverse relationship)
Cardiac output curve plateaus at ~13 L/min (2.5× normal) — the heart's reserve capacity before it becomes the limiting factor.

Hypoeffective heart: ↑arterial pressure, ↓nervous excitation, coronary blockage, valve disease, myocarditis, hypoxia. High CO states: beriberi, AV fistula, hyperthyroidism, anemia (all ↓TPR).

Venous Return Curve

  • VR = (Psf − RAP)/RVR (Psf = mean systemic filling pressure; RVR = resistance to venous return, mostly in veins)
  • At RAP = 0, VR is maximal. As RAP rises, VR falls linearly until VR = 0 at RAP = Psf
  • ↑Blood volume (exercise, RAAS activation, IV fluids) → ↑Psf → curve shifts right → ↑VR
  • Sympathetic venoconstriction → ↓vein distensibility → ↑Psf → ↑VR (most resistance to VR is in the veins, which have high capacitance)

Combined CO/VR Curves & Equilibrium

Combined CO/VR curves — equilibrium point A shifts to B with increased Psf (e.g., exercise, ↑volume)
The equilibrium point is the only point where VR = CO and RAP is equal for both heart and systemic circulation (Frank-Starling equilibrium).

7. Coronary Circulation & Ischemic Heart Disease

  • Normal coronary flow ~225 mL/min (~4–5% of CO); during exercise, work ↑6–9× but flow only ↑3–4× (subendocardial plexus compensates)
  • Coronary flow falls during systole (compression by contracting LV) and rises during diastole (muscle relaxed, no obstruction)
Left vs. right coronary flow across the cardiac cycle
Major regulator of coronary flow = arteriolar resistance via metabolic activity. ↑O₂ demand → local vasodilators released (NO, CO₂, H⁺, K⁺, adenosine) → ↓resistance → ↑flow.

Ischemic Heart Disease & AMI

  • Atherosclerosis → plaque → rupture → thrombus (local occlusion) or embolus (distal occlusion) → infarction downstream
  • Collaterals (20–250 μm anastomoses) dilate within seconds of occlusion but provide <50% needed flow initially; double by day 2–3, near-normal by ~1 month
Cardiac biomarker release timeline post-MI
MarkerTiming
MyoglobinRises earliest, peaks within hours
CK-MBPeaks ~12–16 hrs (useful in NSTEMI, where troponin rise is comparatively low)
TroponinVery high in STEMI, peaks ~1.5–2 days; remains elevated longest
STEMI: ST elevation, ↓R wave amplitude → deepening Q wave → T wave inversion over days-weeks (transmural). NSTEMI: ST depression ± T inversion (subendocardial), lower troponin rise than STEMI.

Symptoms: crushing chest pain radiating to arm/jaw/neck (more common presentation in men); chest heaviness/dyspnea (more common presentation in women); cold clammy skin, grey pallor.

Causes of death post-MI: ↓CO, pulmonary edema (backup into lungs), V-fib (most common cause of sudden death), cardiac rupture (late, from systolic stretch of thinned necrotic wall).

Treatment: Immediate — O₂, aspirin, nitrates, anticoagulants, beta-blockers, ACE-I. Long-term — PCI (stenting), CABG.

Angina

TypePattern
Chronic stablePain with exertion, relieved by rest
UnstablePain at rest AND exertion — higher risk
Variant (Prinzmetal)Coronary vasospasm, often nocturnal/at rest
Treatment: nitrates (1st-line — ↑NO/cGMP → venodilation → ↓preload → ↓wall stress → ↓O₂ demand), CCBs, beta-blockers, ACE-I.

8. Microcirculation & Starling Forces

  • ~10 billion capillaries, 500–700 m² surface area; diffusion is the primary transport mechanism
  • Permeability varies by molecular size and tissue (glomerulus >> BBB)
  • Capillary types: continuous (most tissues, tight junctions), fenestrated (glomerulus, intestine — rapid filtration), sinusoidal/discontinuous (liver, spleen, bone marrow — allow proteins/cells through)

Starling Forces

Net Filtration Pressure = (Pc − Pif) − (πp − πif)
  • Hydrostatic pressures (Pc, Pif) drive fluid OUT of the capillary; oncotic pressures (πp, πif) pull fluid IN
  • 75% of plasma oncotic pressure comes from albumin, 25% from globulins
  • Filtration favored at the arterial end; reabsorption favored at the venous end

Edema

Most common cause of edema = elevated capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) — e.g. heart failure, venous obstruction.
ConditionMechanism
Left heart failureBlood backs up into pulmonary vessels → ↑Pc → pulmonary edema
Right heart failureBlood backs up into systemic veins → ↑Pc in lower extremities/viscera → peripheral edema/ascites
DVT/thrombophlebitis↑upstream Pc → local edema

Local Blood Flow Control

  • Vasodilator (adenosine) theory: ↑metabolism → ↓O₂ + ↑ATP breakdown → ↑adenosine → smooth muscle relaxation
  • Active hyperemia: ↑flow with ↑metabolic activity. Reactive hyperemia: post-occlusion flow surge (4–7×) from accumulated dilator metabolites
  • Autoregulation: intrinsic constant-flow maintenance despite BP changes, independent of nerves/hormones
    • Metabolic theory: waste accumulation → vasodilation; waste clearance → constriction
    • Myogenic theory: sudden ↑pressure/stretch → vessel constricts intrinsically
  • Endothelial factors: NO and PGI₂ = vasodilators; ET-1 (endothelin) = vasoconstrictor

9. Systemic Hemodynamics

Vessel Classification

TypeExamplesFunction
Conducting (elastic) arteriesAorta, carotid, pulmonary trunkExpand in systole, recoil in diastole
Distributing (muscular) arteriesBrachial, femoral, renal, splenicDistribute to organs
Arterioles—Control flow to organs (main resistance vessels)
Veins/venules—Store 60–68% of total blood volume (high capacitance)

Flow, Resistance & Ohm's Law of the Circulation

Q = ΔP/R (flow = pressure gradient / resistance). CO = (arterial − CVP)/R
  • Fick's principle: CO = tissue O₂ consumption / (arterial O₂ − venous O₂)
  • Laminar flow = smooth, layered. Turbulent flow = irregular/mixing — favored by high velocity, large diameter, high density, low viscosity (high Reynolds number, >4000 = turbulent, <2000 = laminar)

Blood Pressure & MAP

  • Normal BP ~120/75–80 mmHg. Pressure = CO × SVR
  • Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic (normal ~40mmHg). Narrow PP → think ↓SV (HF, hypovolemia). Wide PP (≥50mmHg, or in trained athletes) → ↑CV risk
  • MAP = diastolic + 1/3(pulse pressure); normal MAP 70–100 mmHg
  • Pressure falls progressively from aorta (~93 mmHg) → capillaries (~35 mmHg) → right atrium (~2 mmHg)

Peripheral Resistance & Poiseuille's Law

Flow ∝ radius⁴ — vessel radius is the dominant determinant of resistance
  • Resistance depends on: viscosity, vessel length, vessel radius (radius is by far the most powerful — halving radius ↑resistance 16-fold)
  • Resistance in series = sum of resistors (arterioles). Resistance in parallel = reciprocal sum (capillary beds) — parallel network has lower total resistance

10. Neural & Hormonal Regulation of MAP

Autonomic Receptor Summary

Autonomic effector responses, receptors, and signaling pathways
Key receptors: Sympathetic → β1 (heart, ↑rate/contractility via ↑cAMP), α1 (vasoconstriction via ↑PLC/Ca²⁺), β2 (vasodilation in muscle, via epinephrine). Parasympathetic → M2 (SA/AV node, ↓rate via K⁺ channels).

Baroreceptor Reflex

  • Negative feedback loop stabilizing minute-to-minute BP. Carotid baroreceptors respond above 50–60 mmHg, saturate at 180 mmHg. Aortic baroreceptors have a higher threshold, less sensitive
  • ↑BP → baroreceptor stretch → inhibits medullary vasoconstrictor center + excites vagal center → ↓HR, ↓contractility, vasodilation → ↓BP
  • Valsalva maneuver: ↑intrathoracic pressure → ↓preload → ↓baroreceptor firing → ↑sympathetic (↑HR/CO/TPR/MAP) during strain; release → rebound ↑VR/CO/MAP → reflex bradycardia
  • Orthostatic response: standing → venous pooling → ↓VR → ↓CO → ↓MAP → baroreceptor-mediated sympathetic surge restores BP
  • Respiratory sinus arrhythmia: inspiration → ↑HR (vagal inhibition + ↑VR from ↓intrathoracic pressure); expiration → ↓HR (vagal reactivation)

Chemoreceptors & CNS Ischemic Response

  • Carotid/aortic body chemoreceptors activate only when MAP falls below ~80 mmHg; sensitive to ↓O₂, ↑CO₂, ↑H⁺ → ↑sympathetic → vasoconstriction + tachycardia
  • CNS ischemic response: triggered when MAP <60 mmHg — most powerful sympathetic activator, can raise MAP to ~250 mmHg; emergency-only mechanism
  • Cushing reflex/triad (↑ICP): ↑BP, widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular respirations

RAAS Pathway

Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System overview
  • Renin release triggers: ↓Na⁺ delivery to macula densa, ↓renal perfusion pressure (afferent arteriole baroreceptors), sympathetic β1 stimulation of JGA
  • Angiotensinogen (liver) →renin→ Angiotensin I →ACE→ Angiotensin II
  • Angiotensin II effects (AT1 receptors): vasoconstriction (↑TPR/MAP via Gq/PLC/Ca²⁺), ↑thirst, ↑ADH secretion, ↑sympathetic NE release, stimulates aldosterone release
  • Aldosterone (zona glomerulosa) → ↑ENaC + Na/K-ATPase in collecting duct principal cells → Na⁺/water reabsorption
  • ACE inhibitors (ramipril, lisinopril, enalapril) → ↓Angiotensin II → used in HTN and heart failure
  • ANP (released from atrial stretch) is antagonistic to RAAS: dilates afferent arteriole (↑GFR/diuresis), ↓Na⁺ reabsorption (natriuresis), ↓renin/aldosterone/ADH release

11. Cardiac Metabolism (Brief)

  • Heart has an absolute requirement for aerobic ATP production (limited anaerobic capacity) — needed for Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, myosin ATPase, and SR Ca²⁺ transport
  • Postabsorptive fuel mix: ~60–70% fatty acids, ~30% carbohydrates — the heart is metabolically flexible and substrate availability-dependent
  • High ATP/ADP and high NADH/NAD⁺ ratios inhibit fatty acid oxidation (feedback signal that energy needs are already met)
  • In fasting/diabetic states, increased reliance on fatty acid oxidation and ketone body utilization occurs as carbohydrate availability drops
This section is deliberately brief — the biochemical detail of β-oxidation/ketogenesis pathways is lower-yield for the CV/Resp clinical course than the electrophysiology and hemodynamics above; revisit the full source guide if a deeper biochemistry review is needed.
